questions.q: What was the barter system, and what problems led to the invention of money?
answer: The barter system was the direct exchange of goods for other goods or services, without the use of money, and it worked in early, simple societies.

answer.text: Barter faced serious difficulties. It required a double coincidence of wants, meaning each person had to want exactly what the other offered. There was no common measure of value, so it was hard to say how much of one good equalled another. Many goods were indivisible, like a cow that could not be split for small purchases, and perishable goods could not easily store value.
To overcome these problems, money was invented as a common medium of exchange accepted by everyone, making buying, selling and saving far easier.

questions.q: Trace the evolution of money and explain its main functions.

answer.text: Money developed in stages. First came commodity money such as cattle, grain, salt and cowrie shells; then metal coins of gold, silver and copper; then paper currency notes; and finally modern forms like bank money, cards and digital UPI payments.

Money serves four main functions. It is a medium of exchange, accepted by all for buying and selling; a measure of value, giving a common yardstick to price goods; a store of value, since it can be saved for the future; and a standard of deferred payment, used to settle debts and instalments later.

answer: In India the currency is the Rupee, and currency notes are issued by the Reserve Bank of India.
